teach.heading: The instrument is the market. The contract count is your size inside that market.
teach.body: That distinction has to be crystal clear. MNQ, NQ, MGC, ES are instruments — they tell you what market you are trading. 1 contract, 2 contracts, 5 contracts tells you how much exposure you have to that instrument's move. Same market. Different emotional and dollar weight.
teach.dayliNote: Micros keep you teachable — smaller exposure gives you room to actually learn before your emotions hijack the lesson.

experience.intro: Same two instruments, now walked through a few decisions.

steps.prompt: MNQ moves $2/point, MGC moves $10/point. Both move 10 points in your favor while you hold 1 contract each. Which trade made more money?

options.label: The MGC trade — $10/point beats $2/point on the same 10-point move
options.feedback: Right — same move size, bigger per-point value, bigger dollar result.

options.label: They made the same amount
options.feedback: Same points moved, but very different dollar values per point — not the same result.

steps.prompt: Now you take 5 contracts of MNQ instead of 1, same 10-point move. Did you switch instruments?

options.label: No — still MNQ, just more size and more dollar exposure
options.feedback: Exactly — the instrument didn't change, only your exposure to its movement did.

options.label: Yes — more contracts makes it a different instrument
options.feedback: Contract count changes size, not identity. It's still the same instrument.

steps.prompt: A trader with a small account keeps taking 10 MNQ contracts on every setup because "it's just MNQ." What's the risk in that thinking?

options.label: She's ignoring that size changes her dollar risk even though the instrument stays the same
options.feedback: Right — "just MNQ" can still be a big risk if the size is large enough.

options.label: There's no risk — MNQ is a micro, so any size is safe
options.feedback: Being a micro contract doesn't make any size automatically safe — size always matters.

reinforce.question: A trader switches from trading 1 contract of MNQ to 5 contracts of MNQ. Has she changed instruments, and what actually changed about her trade?
options: No — she's still trading the same instrument (MNQ); only her size and dollar exposure changed
Yes — 5 contracts makes it a different instrument entirely
It's impossible to tell without knowing the price

reinforce.question: Two traders both say they're "trading MNQ." One holds 1 contract, the other holds 20. Are they taking the same risk? Explain.
reinforce.modelAnswer: No. They're trading the same instrument, but contract count changes dollar exposure directly — 20 contracts moves 20x the money on the same point move as 1 contract. Same instrument, very different risk.

reinforce.question: Trading more contracts of the same instrument changes your ___, not the instrument itself.
